reasons: B tells the user plainly to send tonight and ties that to the timestamp doing the date-on-record work, while A does the reverse: it denies the send time matters and invites the user to reread it in the morning, which is exactly the delay the user's stated purpose rules out. Both code blocks are complete, placeholder-safe emails, so the drafts are near-equivalent and the timing advice decides it. B's aside about the company reading it whenever they open the inbox is a small claim about reading time, but it argues against delay rather than for it.

A: Claims the damage date is on record "because the body says it" and "not because of the send timestamp", and that delaying the send costs nothing; a self-asserted date in a later email is weaker evidence than a contemporaneous send timestamp, and notice deadlines run from when the notice is actually sent.
B: Says "the claim is already open once this is sent", which overstates the effect: the same email asks the company for the claim forms and deadline, so sending it gives notice rather than opening a claim.
